query: Which differential-privacy epsilon ranges and re-identification-risk bounds are defensible for policing data, and how do we validate synthetic data fidelity and utility?

response.query: Which differential-privacy epsilon ranges and re-identification-risk bounds are defensible for policing data, and how do we validate synthetic data fidelity and utility?
response.answer: For policing data, epsilon ranges typically between 0.1 and 1 provide a balance of privacy and utility. Synthetic data fidelity and utility are validated through statistical comparisons and real-world application testing.

results.title: USENIX Security '25 Technical Sessions
results.content: With a systematic evaluation of diverse methods, our study provides actionable insights into the utilty-privacy tradeoffs of synthetic data generation methods and guides the decision on optimal data releasing strategies for real-world applications. In our evaluation against 15 real-world Java web applications, WDFuzz achieved a 92.6% recall rate in the known vulnerability dataset, finding 3.2 times more vulnerabilities and detecting them 7.1 times faster than the state-of-the-art web fuzzer. In this paper, we design and implement the first framework, called JAEX, to automatically detect and exploit Java Web Application vulnerabilities via concolic execution guided by so-called Cross-thread Object Manipulation. We develop GlitchFHE, an analytical framework that guides toward such adversarial security assessment of FHE applications against FIAs. We run through a set of timely and relevant case studies, covering established applications like image processing, neural networks, and polynomial evaluation, for the prominent CKKS and BFV schemes, both at the analytical/software level and the physical/real-world level.
